appraisal_events.evidence: Jupien reveals that the "Bobette" of the love letters Gilberte intercepted is Morel; the world sees Robert parade women and leave "Mme de Saint-Loup rentrer comme elle pouvait"; at Balbec his short glance at the waiter betrays "un autre plan" in his life that his wife never sees.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narration establishes Robert's concealed life and the deception of his marriage as fact, exposing the exemplary husband as a performance, though it withholds moral condemnation and keeps Jupien's indignation at Morel rather than at him.

appraisal_events.evidence: Having bitterly denigrated her son-in-law, "un beau jour tout avait été changé, le gendre était devenu un ange"; she is paid in rubies for smoothing his way to travel with Morel, and can now "éblouir chaque table où elle allait dîner... d'un luxe inouï" in what the narrator calls "la période de la chasteté finale".
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator traces her reversal of judgment straight back to her need to be kept, discrediting her verdicts while granting that the arrangement leaves her more brilliantly turned out than ever.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Toute la faveur de M. de Charlus s'était portée... sur le jeune marquis de Cambremer", whose tastes, being the baron's own, only made him more appreciated once widowed; his intelligence is "remarquable", but the favour is glossed by whist and the letter signed Léonor betrays the family tic.
appraisal_events.explanation: Charlus takes the young marquis into his intimacy and esteem, a real gain that the narration immediately undercuts by grounding it in shared tastes, card-playing convenience, and inherited mannerism.

appraisal_events.evidence: Bloch "prenait des airs faussement à l'aise" among pretentious young academics, shouted "De ma vie je n'ai jamais su faire un menu" "avec un orgueil peu sincère", upset two water carafes, and ordered champagne "d'une façon tout à fait symbolique"; "Saint-Loup, lui, savait commander."
appraisal_events.explanation: The restaurant vignette holds Bloch up as loud, insincere and clumsy, and the flat comparison with Saint-Loup completes the deflation.

status_effects.explanation: He is shown deceiving and publicly compromising his wife, gone "très sec", and buying his mother-in-law's help; the narration's indulgence keeps the fall moderate.
She is the deceived party who does not know what she is deceived about, jealous of a rival who no longer counts and wearing Rachel's ribbons to hold a husband who cannot want her.
Jupien's indignation falls on him: he left the baron "salement" and used "des ruses diaboliques" to break up the nephew's household.
Her praise and her blame are both shown to be purchasable, and her son-in-law becomes an angel exactly when he becomes her protector.
Inside the world of the passage she is seen dazzling every dinner and every evening with unheard-of luxury and has never been so elegant.
He crosses into the baron's intimacy — the passage names the threshold explicitly, "celui qui l'admet dans son intimité".
He is credited with remarkable intelligence and charm as a companion, even as the narration deflates the grounds of the favour.
The scene leaves nothing of his performance standing: false ease, insincere pride, spilled carafes, and a rival who simply knows how to order.

ambiguities: Aimé's testimony that Saint-Loup's inversion dates back to the first Balbec summer is explicitly contested by the narrator ("ou le liftier avait menti, ou c'était Aimé qui mentait"), so how far back the exposure reaches is left unresolved.
